name: Queensland
summary_text: Queensland is a state within Australia and stands under the national framework: the federal Sex Discrimination Act has protected gender identity since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that this protection extends to trans women as women and awarded damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member; Reuters reported the decision on 23 August 2024 as a national precedent on the exclusion of trans women from services under sex-discrimination law. The dispute arose out of organised exclusionary activism.  Federal hate-crime legislation (Act 1 of 2025) passed in February 2025 and took effect immediately, explicitly covering sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment. Vilification coverage at state level remains uneven across Australia: Queensland is one of the jurisdictions whose law covers gender identity, alongside South Australia and Tasmania, while New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria cover only sexual orientation and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither.  Queensland's own discrimination law strengthened on 29 April 2024, when amendments commenced that moved serious vilification out of the Anti-Discrimination Act and into the Criminal Code, raising the maximum penalty from six months to three years' imprisonment. Those amendments explicitly extend protection to non-binary and gender-diverse people and broaden the definition of gender identity, as stated by the Queensland Human Rights Commission. The Commission has separately presented its account of the Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 rewrite as a modernised gender identity attribute alongside revised vilification provisions.  Queensland was the first Australian state to criminalise conversion practices. The Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passed the Queensland Parliament on 13 August 2020, criminalising electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy practices aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity, with fines and jail time for practitioners. Survivors told SBS the ban does not reach conversion practices in informal, non-healthcare settings.  Entry, facilities and relationship recognition carry no restriction: no Australian law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act 2017 came into force on 9 December 2017 after a 61.6% Yes result in the national postal survey. Federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and overseas same-sex marriages are recognised automatically.  Care access for trans young people is the adverse measure in force for this visit window. In January 2025 Health Minister Tim Nicholls halted puberty blockers and hormone therapy for new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria, formalised by a Queensland Health directive of 28 January 2025 that exempts patients already registered at the Queensland Children's Gender Service. The Queensland Supreme Court ruled the directive unlawful on 27 October 2025; a new ministerial directive reinstated substantially the same restrictions on 28 October 2025 pending reviews, and a legal challenge was filed in December 2025. Equality Australia has called Queensland an outlier state, and families affected by the pause report private treatment costs of hundreds of dollars per injection, approaching $2,000 in one case.  Detention runs on a stated rule with discretion attached. Queensland's inspection standards of August 2023, issued under the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, but staff retain discretion at admission and transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that identity-based process. The 2009 Corrective Services procedure it replaced was assessed as largely ineffective.

sources.documents: Government corruption inquiry leading to formal review recommending decriminalisation of homosexual activity.

name: Tasmania
summary_text: Tasmania stands under the Australian national framework. The federal Sex Discrimination Act has treated gender identity as a protected ground since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. A trans visitor to Tasmania can invoke that federal protection directly, and Tasmania is among the Australian jurisdictions whose vilification law also names gender identity as a protected ground. Federal hate-crime legislation in force since February 2025 expressly covers gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment.  Male homosexual conduct ceased to be criminal in Tasmania with effect from 14 May 1997. The Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act commenced on 19 December 1994, but Tasmania kept its Criminal Code provisions until faced with a likely adverse outcome in Croome v Tasmania, at which point it repealed them and became the final Australian jurisdiction to do so. The age of consent is 17, a threshold shared only with South Australia.  Identity-document rules are permissive. In April 2019 Tasmania's House of Assembly passed the Marriage Amendments Bill on 10 April 2019, after the Legislative Council had already approved it and after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition. The reforms make gender on birth certificates optional, remove any requirement that a transgender person undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised, and allow people aged 16 or over to change their registered gender without parental approval. As of 2019 Tasmania also issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates. The Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out later repeal.  Nothing in the sourced material imposes facility restrictions, medical screening or entry friction on trans travellers to Tasmania. Marriage equality has held nationally since the Marriage Amendment (Definition and Religious Freedoms) Act came into force on 9 December 2017, federal law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto partners since 2009, and Tasmania allows same-sex couples to enter registered domestic partnerships with an optional official ceremony. Same-sex couples have had equal adoption rights in every Australian state and territory since April 2018.  No state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern is documented for Tasmania, and the available evidence for trans equality there is enactment-level rather than case-level.

sources.title: UN Human Rights Committee - Toonen v Australia ruling
sources.documents: International ruling that Tasmania's criminalisation of private same-sex acts violated human rights; triggered federal action
sources.detail: Cited as UN Human Rights Committee ruling in favour of Nicholas Toonen on 31 March 1994, including quote on criminalisation not being reasonable/proportionate to prevent AIDS/HIV spread
